recent_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: Import Maps
recent_posts.summary: Import Maps allow developers to write bare module specifiers like `import thing from "place"` and map them to actual file paths, node_modules, or CDN URLs — eliminating the need for a bundler to resolve dependencies. CodePen's Compiler leverages this by auto-generating import maps so users can write standard npm-style imports without any build setup. The post also covers the limitation of import maps being inline-only (no external file linking), a workaround discovered by Lea Verou, JSPM's similar approach, and Shopify's work to improve adoption including lifting the single-import-map restriction.

recent_posts.title: 424: File List Optimization
recent_posts.summary: CodePen's 2.0 Editor supports hundreds of files per Pen, which can create heavy DOM load and hurt performance. Instead of full virtualization, the team uses IntersectionObserver to detect visibility of file/folder items, freezing off-screen elements and fading them in and out — a lightweight but effective optimization for large file lists with event listeners and drag-and-drop support.

recent_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: ZIP first?
recent_posts.summary: Putting the ZIP code first in address forms could auto-fill city, state, and country from a single input, potentially improving e-commerce checkout conversion rates. However, the approach has real-world complications: it feels unfamiliar to users, requires reliable ZIP code lookup APIs (the demo site's API is currently broken), and ZIP codes vary in format and aren't globally unique, making country-first arguably more correct. Stripe Elements is highlighted as an example of a checkout form that prioritizes conversion but doesn't use this approach. The broader takeaway is that form UX should leverage autocomplete attributes, geolocation, and smart backend processing to reduce friction.

recent_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: URLs
recent_posts.summary: A roundup of interesting URL-related topics: the No-Vary-Search HTTP header that lets site owners tell caches which query parameters actually affect content, a tribute to Flickr's clean and human-readable URL design, and the proposed /.well-known/change-password convention that would let password managers reliably find password-change pages across any site.

recent_posts.title: 422: Supporting Packages
recent_posts.summary: CodePen's 2.0 Editor introduces npm package support by auto-detecting used packages, generating a package.json, and converting it into an importmap script tag that loads modules from esm.sh. The CodePen Compiler handles this pipeline quickly and handles edge cases behind the scenes.

recent_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: Share What You Do
recent_posts.summary: A roundup of developer blog posts worth reading, covering Chrome DevTools performance features, the story behind the Sonner toast component, CSS subgrid usage patterns, accessible faux-nested interactive controls, and a reminder to avoid jargon when writing for mixed audiences. The post celebrates the value of developers sharing their personal workflows, preferences, and ideas openly.

recent_posts.title: 421: View Control of the 2.0 Editor
recent_posts.summary: Stephen and Chris walk through the UI of CodePen's new 2.0 Editor, highlighting the expanded view control options compared to the Classic editor. Topics covered include the default editor layout, the Omnibar (CMD-K), deployment panel, privacy and collaboration settings, details view, minimal UI mode, footer contents, and right-click context menus.

recent_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: Design
recent_posts.summary: A reflective piece on design philosophy touching on perfectionism, simplicity, UI density, and the growing prevalence of AI-generated interfaces. The author expresses fatigue with one-shot AI UIs and argues that true simplicity, intentionality, and good defaults require human taste. Also explores the tension between minimal settings and power-user needs, concluding that thoughtful design means balancing all these considerations simultaneously.

recent_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: Even Grids
recent_posts.summary: A roundup of independent discoveries around the same CSS layout problem: achieving even-height image grids using flexbox and aspect ratios. Multiple developers across different years arrived at similar solutions using flex-grow and pre-calculated aspect ratios. Also covers the 'logo soup' problem of balancing logos with different aspect ratios and visual weights, touches on CSS grid lanes as an emerging standard, and links to additional CSS layout resources.

recent_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: Processing
recent_posts.summary: CodePen's new 2.0 compiler introduces Inline Block Processing, allowing developers to use lang attributes on HTML elements to process content server-side (e.g., Markdown, SCSS) without client-side tools. The post also touches on the no-build-tool philosophy, TypeScript alternatives like JSDoc and ts-check comments, using AI as a pseudo build tool for one-time code conversions, and whether AI could replace a CMS by keeping content directly in the codebase.

top_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: Freshly-Fallen CSS
top_posts.summary: CSS Grid Lanes (formerly masonry) is coming to browsers with a new display property. New CSS features include text-grow and text-shrink for automatic text sizing, and scroll-triggered animations that complement existing scroll-driven animations. Customizable select elements are gaining traction with advanced styling and interactivity options now available in browsers.

top_posts.title: Exploring 21 Unique Custom Cursors for Your Site – CodePen
top_posts.summary: Microinteractions, such as custom cursors, can enhance user experiences by adding uniqueness and interactivity to a site. The post explores various types of custom cursors, including trailing, revealing, and interactive game cursors, along with their implementation techniques using CSS and JavaScript. Performance and accessibility considerations are also discussed. Real-life application examples and relevant CodePen demos provide practical insights for web design and development.

top_posts.title: Liquid glass design trend raises accessibility concerns despite visual appeal
top_posts.summary: The liquid glass design trend is gaining popularity among developers, with CSS implementations using backdrop-filter blur effects to create frosted glass appearances. While visually appealing and demonstrated by Apple in their recent designs, this trend raises accessibility concerns due to poor text contrast ratios. The effect has been around for years but is experiencing renewed interest, with developers creating various implementations and tutorials.

top_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: All Together Now
top_posts.summary: Modern CSS has evolved to handle tasks that previously required JavaScript. Features like custom selects with `appearance: base-select`, anchor positioning, scroll-driven animations, and scroll state queries now enable complex UI patterns purely in CSS. When combined, these capabilities demonstrate CSS's transformation into a more powerful, intelligent language that covers most presentation and interaction needs without JavaScript.

top_posts.title: Chris’ Corner: Cursors
top_posts.summary: CSS provides built-in cursor styles that can enhance user experience when applied thoughtfully. OS-supplied cursors support accessibility features like size adjustments, while custom cursors can create problems. The article explores cursor best practices, highlighting how tools like Figma extend cursor functionality with contextual information, preview states, and collaborative features without replacing the default cursor entirely.
